title: $\pi$-Bench: Evaluating Proactive Personal Assistant Agents in Long-Horizon Workflows
claim: A benchmark combines user personas, multi-session episodes with dependencies, a shared persistent environment, and dual proactivity and completeness metrics.
layout: 4 panels (a–d), left-to-right, color-coded headers, formulas in evaluation panel
description: A wide four-panel figure with rounded, color-coded panels. Panel a (blue) lists five user roles (Researcher, Marketer, Law Trainee, Pharmacist, Financier) as icon cards, with a person icon and the counts 5 roles and 100 tasks. Panel b (dark green) shows an episode as a timeline of sessions S1 to S20, with curved arrows for cross-session dependencies. A legend separates dependent sessions from independent ones. Panel c (olive) shows the persistent project environment. A row of workspace resources (files, memory, tools, skills, artifacts) sits above a flow from Initial Request to Evaluated Agent to User Agent, with a feedback loop. Below it, a Hidden Intent Tracker marks intents as completed, inferred or provided. Panel d (teal) defines the Proactivity and Completeness metrics with fraction formulas and two grader types, rubric-based and rule-based.
caption: Overview of π-BENCH.
abstract: The rise of personal assistant agents, e.g., OpenClaw, highlights the growing potential of large language models to support users across everyday life and work. A core challenge in these settings is proactive assistance, since users often begin with underspecified requests and leave important needs, constraints, or preferences unstated. However, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate whether agents can identify and act on such hidden intents before they are explicitly stated, especially in sustained multi-turn interactions where user needs emerge gradually. To address this gap, we introduce $Ï$-Bench, a benchmark for proactive assistance comprising 100 multi-turn tasks across 5 domain-specific user personas. By incorporating hidden user intents, inter-task dependencies, and cross-session continuity, $Ï$-Bench evaluates agents' ability to anticipate and address user needs over extended interactions, jointly measuring proactivity and task completion in long-horizon trajectories that better reflect real-world use. Experiments show (1) proactive assistance remains challenging, (2) a clear distinction between task completion and proactivity, and (3) the value of prior interaction for proactive intent resolution in later tasks.
